reception.text: The Billings drawing was national wire news, described as another of the government's famous land lotteries, with landseekers arriving from all over the country.
A Kansas City Star piece warned readers the farms were not free: a unit of forty-seven and a half acres would cost more than $1,550 in installments.
Two days into the filing period, a Billings dispatch counted only about twenty entries out of a possible 400.

political_impact.text: The Billings land office received 5,491 applications before the June 25 deadline, many from Billings residents who only wanted to see what number they would draw.
political_impact.source: Timothy A. Dick, Huntley Project (Bureau of Reclamation, 1996), p. 16

political_impact.text: Of the first 1,000 names drawn, only 76 completed filing.
political_impact.source: Timothy A. Dick, Huntley Project (1996), p. 16

political_impact.text: By mid-1908, 238 of the project's 585 farm units, covering 10,675.60 acres, had been entered.
political_impact.source: Reclamation Service, Seventh Annual Report (1907–08), p. 105

political_impact.text: Congress gave the July 1907 entrymen until May 15, 1908 to establish residence.

legacy.text: Only 4,100 acres were irrigated in the 1908 season, and the project went on to drainage trouble and the farm collapse after 1918.
The irrigators organized the Huntley Irrigation District in 1921 and took over operation of the works.

today.name: Huntley Project
today.note: Federal reclamation project east of Billings, run by the Huntley Irrigation District; can water about 30,000 acres.
today.source: Bureau of Reclamation, Huntley Project page

related.note: The Huntley tracts were held back from this 1906 opening of the ceded Crow lands because they had been withdrawn for reclamation.

uncertain: How many names were drawn is unclear: wire stories said 1,500, the Reclamation Service's report says 1,000.

political_impact.text: A General Land Office circular signed by Acting Commissioner Fred Dennett sent the proclamation to the Devils Lake land office, announcing the remaining land open at not less than $2.50 an acre, cash, plus the usual fees.
The Interior Department ruled that land under entry on June 8, 1907 stayed at $4.50 an acre even if the entry was later cancelled.
political_impact.source: Otto A. Kayser and William H. Meyer, cited in 39 L.D. 434–436

legacy.text: A federal appeals court held that the 1904 act's cession language, standing alone, did not show a clear intent by Congress to disestablish the Devils Lake Reservation.
legacy.source: United States v. Grey Bear, 828 F.2d 1286 (8th Cir. 1987)

related.note: Cut the $4.50-an-acre price set for the 1904 Devils Lake opening to $2.50 for land still unsold.

later_actions.text: In Clara F. Moran the Interior Department refused a refund, holding that the price cut reached only land unreserved and undisposed of on June 8, 1907.
The Eighth Circuit ruled in United States v. Grey Bear that the 1904 act alone did not disestablish the Devils Lake Reservation (later vacated in part on other grounds).

uncertain: Who proposed the price cut, and how settlers and the local press received it, is not known.
How many acres sold at the reduced price is not known; the Devils Lake land office's cash-sale abstracts (National Archives Record Group 49) would settle it.

reception.text: Only a handful of people turned up when registration opened at Pierre, since the order of registering had no bearing on the drawing; about 500 registered the first day.
With a day of registration left the total stood at 3,460, and local notaries were angry at outside notaries taking affidavits on the trains.

political_impact.text: The General Land Office judged the registration-and-drawing plan entirely satisfactory and reported that practically all the lands were entered by people who registered.
political_impact.source: General Land Office, Annual Report for 1908, p. 29

legacy.text: Part of the 1906 cession was still unsold in 1913. No court ruling on the present legal status of the cession has been found.

later_actions.text: Woodrow Wilson's Proclamation 1252 offered the unsold lands at public auction at Pierre, for cash, at no less than a dollar an acre.

uncertain: The congressional record read shows no separate assent by the Lower Brule to the House's substitute text of the 1906 act; the agreement's own text, presumably in S. Rep. 253, was not read.
The present legal status of the 1906 Lower Brule cession has not been settled by any ruling found.

political_impact.text: The Lower Brule, the Crow, and the Sisseton, Wahpeton, and Cut-Head bands, who bore the loss of land, had little voice in the newspapers of 1907.

legacy.text: The reduced reservations and mixed ownership these openings left behind are part of the pattern behind a century of litigation over what remains Indian country, though neither Rosebud Sioux Tribe v. Kneip (1977) nor McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) concerned these statutes.
